CANADA POST CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on a matter that has caused a great deal of frustration and alarm in the city of Hamilton. All past Governments regarded regular mail delivery as an essential service which was guaranteed to all Canadians. This is not the case with the present Conservative Government. The deterioration of postal service in my riding and throughout Canada is indicative of the Government's stop-at-nothing attitude when it comes to cost-cutting.
Over the past few months my constituency office has been bombarded with complaints about poor mail service in Hamilton and the increasing number of occasions when there is no mail delivery. In the past two years 80 full-time positions have been eliminated. This has resulted in greater delays, more complaints, and an intensification of the negative view of Canada Post. On any given day 600 to 700 households in Hamilton do not receive their mail. People like Dawn Walker, Patrick and Sharon Le Donne, and Cheryl Seth are frustrated when they do not get their mail, and become incensed when they are told they can pick it up at the post office. As taxpayers these people have a right to regular household delivery.
Mothers, pensioners, and families on welfare are literally living from day-to-day and waiting for cheques that do not arrive because postal service has been stopped. Does the Government have no sense of how critical the prompt delivery of mail is? I had initially planned to mail my complaint to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote). However, because the arrival of such a letter is no longer guaranteed, I stand in this House to call upon the Government to cease its neglect of Canada Post.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the case of a woman, a landed immigrant since 1972, who is now being threatened with deportation.
Mrs. Weinroth still has permanent resident status, but an Immigration Officer in the Montreal area decided to interpret the Immigration Act and Regulations very strictly and is trying to have her status revoked.
Mrs. Weinroth was educated in Quebec from 1969 to 1979. Her family lives in Montreal. Her father teaches at McGill and her mother at Dawson College.
In 1979, she went to Michigan to continue her studies, and she had two children there. Since then, she decided to return to Canada but is now being threatened with deportation. Pending a decision on her case by an arbitration officer, I think it is unfair to threaten Mrs. Weinroth with deportation. She is now battling the U.S. courts for custody of her children, and 1 think the last thing she needs is to be worried as well about being prevented from taking up residence in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is of the utmost urgency to deal with this case and ensure that residents and permanent residents can feel safe and secure. At a time when family re-unification is the order of the day, I think it should be relatively easy to deal with Mrs. Weinroth's case.

SOCIAL SECURITY
subsubtopic: PHILOSOPHY OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a recent interview with Le Devoir, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) presented his Government's blueprint for creating a society of "haves" and "have-nots". He said: "Canada must rethink its social philosophy."
The social philosophy we hold provides all Canadians with certain rights and services, such as medicare and old age pensions, and certain safeguards against the vagaries of a capitalist economy, such as unemployment insurance and

January 29, 1986
income security programs. It is not a perfect system but it is a good philosophy which most Canadians are proud of and support. Our Prime Minister now says we can no longer afford this philosophy. He would have us embrace a pre-Depression philosophy which offers programs, through a means test, to the deserving poor, and relies heavily on voluntary charities such as food banks. He wants quiet consultation, but no embarrassing public debate or political confrontation. He forgets that social policy consultants claim Tory consultation was a farce since their views were ignored.
Instead of listening to consultants and the Canadian public, the Prime Minister relies on the Nielsen recommendations to cut all programs except the military. He allows his hatchet man to develop a new social philosophy, not Canadians.

subtopic: RAILWAYS
RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the derailment of a CP Rail train yesterday near Raith, not far from Thunder Bay, focuses the problems we face in ensuring safe train movement. The derailment, which fortunately occurred in a sparsely-populated area, was the result of a roller bearing burn out. This happened 45 kilometres past one hot box detector and 10 kilometres short of the next one. The technological problem is that burn outs occur more rapidly with roller bearings than with steel axles in brass seats. This means roller bearings fail with very little warning. One of the recommendations of the Grange Inquiry into the Mississauga derailment was that roller bearings should be installed on all tank cars. That recommendation is now in question.
The railway companies have sought approval to do away with cabooses and replace end-of-train crew members with an End-of-Train Information System which is to provide all the monitoring and supervision which crew members presently provide. That now appears more and more dubious.
I call upon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to institute a thorough investigation of these technological challenges. Derailment of trains, especially in the winter-time, appear to be inevitable in our rail transportation system. Let us be sure that on the trains and elsewhere we have all the means to deal with them as safely as possible.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF BELL AIRE SHIPYARD IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people who used to work in the shipyards in British Columbia must be wondering what they have done to incur the wrath of the Conservative Government. The reason given for the announced closure of B.C. Marine Shipbuilders was that the company could no longer wait for the federal Government to deliver on its campaign promises to provide the industry with a policy designed to foster its growth. In fact, if it were not for an accident with a Fisheries Department ship, the workers at B.C. Marine Shipbuilders would already be on unemployment and a padlock would now be on the gates.
Now, more bad news for British Columbia courtesy of the Mulroney Government. The Bell Aire Shipyard in British Columbia will close its doors on Friday. Sixteen months after its election to office, the federal Tory team can point to the accomplishment that at least 728 shipyard workers in three B.C. yards have lost their jobs or are about to pick up their last pay cheques.
Nationally the number of shipyard workers who have the Government to thank for UIC instead of a regular salary runs into the thousands. Why does the Government not do the proper thing and assist shipyards in British Columbia and elsewhere to build ships needed for Canadian purposes?
Unions and the shipyard owners across the land speak in one voice. They told the Government well over a year ago that the Canadian shipbuilding industry could put 40,000 Canadians to work if only the Government would announce the policy it promises so often when it is seeking votes.
Is it too much for B.C. shipyard workers to expect the Government to live up to its promises? Shame on the Tories!

Mr. Speaker, 20 insurance companies agreed to form a voluntary association in Ontario to provide liability insurance to small businesses and non-profit organizations that cannot otherwise get coverage. This group should be praised, but they cover a maximum of only a million dollars in liability insurance, which is not enough to help a Windsor, Ontario, machine tool manufacturing company with 300 employees needing $5 million liability product insurance.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. Yesterday's Ontario Government's report showed, through the use of independent monitoring, what previous Government tests had not. Not only do residents of southwestern Ontario face the threat of inundation by dioxin-containing flood waters but they are drinking dioxin-containing waters right now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the short answer is that we will be introducing a new Environmental Contaminants Act that will address all the concerns that the Hon. Member raised which are within federal jurisdiction. Some of them, of course, are within provincial and municipal jurisdictions.
I should caution the Member, however, that even though we are very concerned, as is the Ontario Government, he should put this matter into perspective. It is not a matter of finding something in the water that was not there before. It is a matter, instead, of science reaching the point where it can detect certain things that could not be detected before. In fact, if one were to express the quantity of the substance found in terms of time instead of weight, it would be equivalent to one second in 32 centuries. In short, it is minute, it is sporadic, and it is not harmful.

There are some items in the report we agree with. However, there are a number of items with which we profoundly disagree. As a result, we issued a minority report pointing out some of the areas where we disagree.
I want to say that I consider the time provided for the committee by this House, which really means by the Government, was not sufficient for the committee to hold hearings in other parts of Canada in order to hear all or even most of the witnesses who wanted to appear. Believe it or not, on an issue as large as this, affecting the entire economy and every region of this country, we did not have as witnesses the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association. The length of time provided for people to prepare submissions and give notice was inadequate, and that was not the fault of the committee. I want to say here and now, Sir, that all members of the committee worked diligently and long, hard hours trying to cover a subject of this size in the limited time provided.
The question which is really at stake here is that of deregulation or re-regulation or a new regulatory regime, whichever expression one chooses to use. I notice there has been much more use of the words "a new regulatory regime" over the last few weeks than there had been all last summer. Whatever you call it, we responded last August to the Government White Paper called Freedom to Move. We called it "Freedom to Manoeuvre", because it states it is:
"a trial balloon of Conservative ideology which solves fewer problems for the transportation industry than it will create. Clearly there are no pressing issues facing the transportation industry which call for actions by the Minister like those proposed in his policy paper". These proposals are for sweeping deregulation where there is no apparent need, and that clearly indicates that the paper is only a knee-jerk regurgitation of similar transportation initiatives undertaken in the U.S. by President Reagan and President Carter.

Our participation in this process-

speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I hate to interrupt the Hon. Member on his excellent delivery, but it appears the Liberals have abandoned the House. Is there a particular reason?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And they are sitting with their natural allies, Mr. Speaker.
If I may continue, participation by members of the New Democratic Party in this whole process on the Government's White Paper has confirmed our long-held belief that there is some room for substantial improvement in Canada's transportation sector. The current regulatory environment is often cumbersome, inappropriate in some areas, and does not always produce the results intended. We recognize that in a changing world, in a changing transportation environment, regulations must keep pace. They must reflect the world of today and not of yesterday.
Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker. Unless it has been changed and I do not know about it, under the House of Commons Act, the Constitution Act or whatever, there is still a regulation that while Members of Parliament are provided with free railway transportation, I am still entitled to check my horse in the baggage car. That is a regulation held over from before 1867 which I believe is still in place. However, if we continue down the slippery slope of deregulation, as this Government proposes, I may have to check my horse so I can get from Winnipeg to Regina in a couple or three days.
We agree that we have to propose transportation policies for the 1980s and 1990s in keeping with the nature and history of our country. Transportation policy is a policy that recognizes the important role of the private sector but that maintains the predominance of the public interest rather than private profit in directing the development of Canada's transportation sector. In essence, it has to be a policy based on re-regulation, not deregulation.
We believe the time has come for upgrading and updating our regulatory regime. We agree that the Canadian Transport Commission should be modernized and updated, its powers strengthened, its methods of operation streamlined, and that it should be more responsive to the consumer and the users of transportation in a shorter space of time than has been the experience in the past.
Much of the distrust or disbelief in the activities of the CTC over the last many years has occurred because there is a suspicion, not ill-founded, that whatever the railways or the airlines wanted they got one way or the other and sooner or later. There was not sufficient attention paid or response given
to the needs of shippers and receivers or to consumers who pay the final price.
We feel that the sixth report of the Transport Committee, the minority report which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), and I submitted, and I believe a report from the Liberal Party, should be considered only as interim reports.
We feel that the House of Commons, with the approval of the Government, should extend the reference to the Transport Committee for further study, including permission to conduct public hearings in northern Canada and other outlying communities in southern Canada, and that the Committee be allowed to travel to the United States to gather information with respect to the Americans' experience with transportation deregulation, the number one recommendation in our minority report. The Government of Canada should undertake to have a complete independent market analysis and impact study done of the expected results of deregulation in Canada, the known results and effects of deregulation in the United States concerning all modes of transportation, including the effect on safety, security and employment prior to the drafting of any legislation.
The Government should increase funding immediately, in fact even retroactively if necessary, to provide for more inspection services, not only for the inspection and supervision of regulations regarding maintenance, safety procedures and so forth, but also of their enforcement.
If I may illustrate, Mr. Speaker, the present Government is doing no more than extending what the previous administration started with its restraint programs in 1975-1976.
Let us just look at air mode person years. Specifically, let us take general technical inspectors. The number of them for 1985-86 is 390, down 23 from 1984-85. On technical inspection-the people out on the ground-the number for 1985-86 is 201, down from 223 for 1984-85.
With or without deregulation, there is a growing volume of people travelling, a growing volume of aircraft, trucks, buses and cars in our transportation system. With or without deregulation, Sir, you have to enlarge the capability of your regulatory bodies and of the Department of Transport to inspect and enforce the regulations that are there for public safety and security.
You cannot have it both ways. I do not know of a single taxpayer of any political stripe anywhere in Canada who says that we are spending too much in the area of inspection and enforcement of regulations. In fact, taxpayers would support an increase in expenditures in that area. This nonsense about across-the-board reductions in order to satisfy the hypnotic influence of deficits is, I think, a disservice and is false economy. There are some areas in which you do not, I repeat, do not reduce expenditures. There are areas in which they must be increased. That is an area in which no Government with any conscience or feeling of responsibility could either allow or stand for reductions.
January 29, 1986

In a new regulatory regime, a re-regulated regime or a deregulated regime, a comparison of Canada with the United States is odious, as the old saying goes. The drafters of the White Paper overlooked the fact that that country has 10 times the population and more than 10 times the volume of traffic, both people and goods to move, in a smaller geography and in a milder climate. That in itself speaks volumes as to the applicability of their experience or ideological bent in Canada. The only parts of Canada which are readily comparable with the United States are the Quebec-Windsor corridor, if we are talking about rail and trucking, and Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, and once in a while Edmonton, Calgary and Halifax. They are the only ones which are comparable. This means that three-quarters of the geography of Canada is left out, that cities such as Lethbridge, Regina, Saskatoon, Thunder Bay, North Bay, Timmins, London and Moncton are left out. If we found out anything in Washington last week, it was that deregulation in 20 cities meant a return to mediocrity and that smaller centres receive a lower quality of service. Although they sometimes received increased frequency, we are now being told that they are prepared to take 100 of those 200 cities, put them under the new regulatory regime and add 100 different cities because of what they have experienced. What applies in the United States does not apply here because most of Canada, in terms of transportation economics, is uneconomical.
In 1867 we decided that we would be a nation and that the nation as a whole would share in an equitable manner from coast to coast, from the forty-ninth parallel to the North Pole, in the cost of providing a reasonable degree of quality, safe and equitable service, and that the routes which were uneconomical would be covered both by taxpayers and by those routes which were economical. For all the criticism about cross-subsidization, if there is one thing that has worked reasonably well, it is the fact that we had, and in most cases still have an economical degree of service. If we looked at only the straight economics of it, we would pull out and leave it to jerkwater, fly by night operators who enter and exit whenever they please. Taxpayers have spent hundreds of millions of dollars on infrastructure, but under the freedom to move provision transporters can come in and pull out whenever they like. This is not only unfair to the transportation consumers who live in the communities, it is unfair to the airline or the trucking company which has built up the infrastructure and has serviced the communities for years. Such a company could have loyal customers and could have built up the business, but someone else can come in and out and skim the cream off the top. That is not free enterprise, that is not fair enterprise. It is nothing more than the worst kind of disservice to the people of the country and to our nationhood. If that is what the Government means by freedom to move-

speechtext: It is not in our report.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Freedom to move is very plain. If there is one thing sure about freedom to move, it is the freedom to
Committee Reports
enter and exit. I admit that even the minority reports are lacking because we did not have enough time to go into that matter. However, we heard evidence from witnesses who told us what would happen.
What applies to a smaller or middle-sized city in the United States of 300,000 to 600,000 people applies to a community in Canada of some 5,000 to 20,000 people. That is the proportion. In the name of free enterprise, those who promote it and want freedom to move say that we can have champagne ideas in a beer market, in a market which will perhaps allow one or two airlines or trucking companies to break even or make a buck and provide a reasonable service. They believe that anyone can come in, divide it up in four or five ways and take turns going broke, take turns entering and exiting.
I do not want Air Canada or PWA to exit from the Cities of Regina, London, Moncton or Gander. They have provided a service in good and bad times. I resent the outfits or the johnny-come-latelies that want to start up airlines or trucking companies coming in for a few months of the year, skimming the cream off the top, and then existing. The company or business which was there in the first place is then left holding the bag and is forced to exit. In that event we end up with another area where we return to mediocrity in terms of quality, quantity and service, which we should work at to provide for every region of the country.
If it were left to free market forces, we might as well vacate three-quarters of the geography of our country, move to Vancouver, Montreal or perhaps a couple of other spots, and let the rest of it sit there. That is not what we are about, and we never have been. I do not suggest for a moment that that is how the Minister feels, but it is inevitable if it is left to free market forces or to so-called will of the market. When something like transportation, which is an essential public utility, essential to the public good and the national well-being, is left to the so-called free market forces, a major part of the country and at least half of our population will not be as well served as they were in the past, despite the warts and things which were not as good as we would have liked.
I am not denying that improvements and changes could be made, but I hope the Government considers the minority reports as interim reports and lets us continue our work. The topic is too large for us to report on it in a matter of three months or four months. I am not suggesting six years or seven years, as was suggested by the MacPherson Royal Commission, but we should have a year or a year and a half at most. We need another year before a new national transportation Act is brought before the House so that the seven provinces and two territories will have a chance to be heard and to present their views. Then we can say that we did a full and a more complete job.

ment of goods in this country as well as what the impact on the consumers will be.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, time did not permit me to get to every mode of transportation. I appreciate my colleague reminding me. Confidential rates are anti-competitive, antifree enterprise and anti-free market. Confidential rates fly in the face of the principles espoused by my hon. friends opposite. Confidential rates provide advantages for large shippers and receivers. They mean exactly that, small shippers and receivers, manufacturers and processors will not be able to find out what those rates are. In actual practice confidential rates leads to corporate raiding. They can lead to fraud and bribery. I suppose that to get a piece of a $5 million market, a $5,000 or $50,000 little bribe would get you the information from a freight traffic manager from your competitor. But it flies in the fact of our principles.
We suggest that we broaden the whole principle of agreed charges in which you require railroads and trucking companies to compete, that one railroad or one trucking company cannot have the same agreed charges as another, and that the small shipper should have has exactly the same opportunity as a large shipper under a system of agreed charges. Under a system of confidential rates that a small shipper, receiver, processor and manufacturer would not get the same kind of deal. The Freedom to Move provisions even propose that you could have a confidential rate if you are a big boy and a big railroad or a big trucking company, and they would allow for rebates. That is the same as kickbacks. Under the former provisions of the Criminal Code that was illegal, but that is allowed it is foreseen, under confidential rates. You allow a rebate, a kickback. If that is free enterprise, I do not want any part of it. If that is taking part in the free market forces, that is nonsense, that is piracy if I ever saw it.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I want to congratulate the Member who has just spoken for raising before the Canadian public his legitimate concerns about deregulation in particular on the air side. I want to say to the Member that he knows, as do all members of the committee, that one of the primary reasons there were minority reports on this government document called Freedom to Move, the Minister's white paper, was the fact that many members of the committee, and particular those in my Party and his Party, believed that the committee had not done its full homework. He knows that, for example, ignoring the U.S. deregulation experience south of the border, doing no research, making no visits, talking to no officials, doing no exploration was almost an act of extreme irresponsibility on the part of the committee, as was the presumption that and then presuming it could comment intelligently on deregulation for Canada.
Last week the Member who has just spoken, myself and a number of Members from the Conservative Party, who are also members of the Transport Committee, had an opportunity, through another vehicle, an exchange program, to be in Washington and to talk to many people who are experts in the field; Congressmen who are chairmen and vice-chairmen of various committees concerned, Republicans and Democrats,
industry people, consultants and so on. I want to ask the Member whether he came away from that experience with the kind of feeling that I had. Whatever my reservations about freedom to move and unfeetered deregulation being introduced in Canada on the air side, I was not prepared for the kind of horror stories we heard in Washington. I came away with one compelling desire, and that is, to ask the Minister and the Government to make provision for the entire committee to go back down to Washington and repeat the program, hopefully in more detail, that Members of Parliament who were there last week went through. I believe that all Members, regardless of Party stripe, can benefit greatly from a visit to Washington, and perhaps will come back with some very strong and clear signals for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) before he proceeds with this deregulation package, in particular as it pertains to the air side. I would like to hear the Hon. Member's comments, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I suppose the one feeling I had even before we left was it was that something of a sad commentary on our parliamentary system as it is functioning at present that we had to rely on an outside organization to see to it that some of us on all sides of the House got down to Washington for three days last week to the centre for parliamentary exchange, which was financed mostly by private contributions. I am sure my colleagues who were with me are as appreciative as I am of that opportunity. Three days was not enough time. We were only able to look at the air side. It did prove to me, Sir, that we need many days, not only to continue our study of the air side but also of the whole area of trucking, railroads, freight rates, marine. We have just scratched the surface, and that is why our main recommendation-I can remind my colleague in the Liberal Party-is that these be considered as interim reports, and that the House of Commons, at the behest of the Government, grant us an extended period of time to continue our hearings and bring in another report several months down the road in which we will have had an opportunity to look at the U.S. experience.
I recall what witnesses in Halifax, Stephenville and a few other places in Newfoundland had to say about the situation in Maine and Minnesota where the population is thin, there is a northern type of climate, and the communities are small, and what their experience there was. There are a couple of states, for example, the experiences of which are applicable to most of Canada. We need to have a lot more insight into and examination of those areas than we have had. I am not faulting the members of the standing committee, Sir, they all worked very hard, and so did the staff. We did not have enough time, and we all know it. We all need to go at this some more. I hope the Government will agree to that.

I would like to ask a question to the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). In view of the question from the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), two Members who were very involved in the Transport Committee, I have some comments to make about his interesting remarks that led off the motion to concur
January 29, 1986

in the sixth report of the Transport Committee, notwithstanding the fact that both opposition Parties walked out when the crunch came and we were supposed to vote. I will come to that later. My question is directed to the Hon. Member for Regina West: What hat was he wearing when he replied to the question from the Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe, the hat of Doctor Jekyll or the one of Mr. Hyde? In his remarks he talked about how the United States was so different. Then he got the set-up question from his friend about the American experience. So really, will he cut the wheat from the chaff? If the American experience is so different, and if in the American experience there is no CN and no Air Canada, nor are there recommendations from the sixth report, which are not even anywhere in the deregulation environment in the United States, why is he even wasting time in this House by talking about the American experience?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was not me or the New Democratic Party who used the United States as an example. We have been confronted continually from day one since the White Paper came down about the glories and the nirvana of deregulation in the United States. We have had it from Hon. Members in this House, people in the transportation sector of this country and the media. It was not we who started that. If the example that has been put to us time and time again since last July is such a good example, then surely it is incumbent upon the Government and the Parliament of Canada to see to it that if there is any validity to the American deregulation experience and if it is applicable to Canada, we should damned well look into it and report back to Parliament about it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult for a relatively junior Member such as I to speak after an Hon. Member with the experience and the great oratorical skills of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has spoken. He was so articulate in putting the case. Indeed, the Hon. Member is absolutely correct. It is the Government of Canada that has been telling members of the Standing Committee on Transport and indeed the population of Canada over these last number of months not to worry about the negative effects of deregulation and to look at the success story in the United States.
We were led to believe that people in the United States were so excited and in such a state of nirvana about the great positive effects of deregulation, particularly on the air side, that they were flying without the benefit of wings. Reality was a sobering experience for Members of Parliament of all three Parties when they arrived in Washington last week.
Since many of us come from outlying regions, perhaps we had a bit of a regional bias about deregulation. Perhaps we were concerned that it would be beneficial to highly populated areas and not so beneficial to less populated areas. We went to Washington expecting to hear from American politicians and chairmen of aviation committees, both Republican and Democrat, that there is some dichotomy in their point of view. We felt that Democrats might be a little critical of deregulation
Committee Reports
and Republicans might say that it was a wonderful thing. That is not what happened.
Going to Washington was a frightening experience for Hon. Members from both sides of the House of Commons. The reality of the deregulation experience in the United States versus the scenario that has been painted for Canadians by the Minister and his officials are as different as day and night.
We have been told that fares have generally decreased throughout the United States air industry system and that consumers have been the big beneficiaries of deregulation. That is all we have been told. When we talk about safety, the Government says: "Don't talk about safety, we are engaging in economic deregulation, not deregulation of safety, so let us not talk about it". When we talk about the nature of Canada and the fact that it is a nation of 25 million people spread over the second largest land mass in the world, the Government says: "Don't worry about that. The free market will determine that Canadians are served somehow, some way no matter where they live".
What was the reality of the American experience? The United States is a country with a population 10 times the population of Canada. We heard some very frightening and alarming testimony from the people to whom we spoke in Washington. The American Government's own report produced by the Office of General Accounting on November 6, 1985, indicates that between 1979 and 1984, the airlines in the United States lost $4 billion. Listening to the horror stories of airlines popping up one day and disappearing the next, airlines going bankrupt and fly-by-nighters appearing and disappearing was akin to imagining a crap shoot. That is the way airline services were being provided to the people of the United States.
The same report indicated that more small communities will likely lose air services when federal subsidies end in 1988. Those small communities still getting air services are getting them because of federal subsidies. That is the American Government's own report.
American Congressmen did a wise thing. They went out into the country to hear from people who had been affected by the airline deregulation, the nirvana that has been described by Hon. Members opposite on occasion. What did the people have to say about it? I have a statement here from the mayor of a typical small American community. In the United States, a small community is one with a population of 50,000 to 200,000. Where I come from, when we talk about a population of
200,000	we are talking about the capital. When we are talking about a population of 50,000, we are talking about a city. When we are talking about a population of 10,000, we are talking about a good sized town. However, in the United States small centres have populations of 50,000 to 200,000.
Peggy Mensinger, the Mayor of the City of Modesto, California, when talking about airline deregulation, had this to say:
In a little over three years and six airlines later, we now have a pure jet airline service back and have hopes of restoring the market that the four bankrupt commuters destroyed. Our enplanements dropped from a peak of 57,000 in 1977 to just over 21,000 in 1982 as a result of deregulation.

January 29, 1986
Committee Reports
She talked about these great commuter airlines which are supposed to replace the jets, something about which the Minister speaks so fondly. It was supposed to be a new type of industry. This is what she had to say about those commuter airlines:
Public rejection of the small commuter aircraft plus fourteen schedule changes in the eighteen months, frequent cancellations, and little or no concern for the passengers caused our annual enplanements to drop from 38,236 in 1979 to 29,750 in 1980.
A U.S. Congressman appearing before the committee which was looking at the effects of airline deregulation spoke of the plight of small rural communities. He said:
We have had one airline after another, attempting to replace the service United abandoned, go bankrupt or get into severe financial difficulties so that service has been disrupted or reduced.
All of the newly-designated EAS carriers have started off well, but something happens to them after that-they begin expanding too fast, their management may have miscalculated their expenses, a recession hits. All of these factors have hurt, not only the airlines attempting to provide service but also the harried Valley air passenger.
Again, statistics provided by the General Accounting Office in the United States show us that in the smaller centres with populations of 50,000 to 200,000, 82 community airports have lost all service. Nothing is flying, propellor or jet. In several hundred more small communities, there has been a dramatic reduction in the level of service. One might say that that is a small price to pay for deregulation because there has been a reduction in fares for people who live in the larger centres.
Let me tell the House what else happened as a result of deregulation. While there was a reduction in air fares in the larger centres and heavily travelled runs of the United States, the runs that would be the equivalent of the Toronto to Montreal run, in the smaller centres and the less travelled routes, there was a corresponding increase in fares. There now exists the anomaly in the United States of one being able to fly on certain days of the week with certain package deals from New York to Los Angeles for $99, no frills, in a plane on which I would not sit, while one can fly from New York City to a town in New York State, only a couple of hundred miles away, for $300. There is now an anomaly which exists in the United States where there is a three-point system. On a carrier which flies from point A to point B to point C the cost of a ticket to fly from point A to point B is $250. The cost is only $150 to fly to points A, B and C. Thus people flying to the point B destination buy a ticket to point C, the farthest destination on the route, get off at point B and throw away the coupon. Where is the fairness in that type of system?
There is another big, bad word which the Minister and Hon. Members do not want us to talk about. It is safety. They say: "Don't worry about safety. Let's not talk about it".

speechtext: What are you talking about? It's the most important element of it.

Every single individual we talked to in the United States, such as representatives of the major airline
carriers, in particular, the President of the Airline Association of the country, Paul Ignatius, the Republican Vice-Chairman of the Aviation Committee from New York, Representative Molinari, the Democratic Deputy Chairman, James Oberstar, the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Aviation in Congress, Congressman Mineta, people we heard in confidence at closed-door meetings, such as the Vice-President of one of the major American airlines-every single person we talked to told us that safety in the American airline industry has suffered. Nobody wants to advertise that fact. No one wants to tell people that it is less safe than it was before. An industry which used to operate far and away, above and beyond the standards set by the Federal Aviation Administration, operates, we now see, at the fringe of the minimum requirements on safety required by the FAA. Congressman Molinari from New York said that in his judgment the airlines are now operating below the minimum standards.
Just how strongly does he feel about this subject? On November 14, 1985 he wrote a letter to the President of the United States, a letter signed by 77 members of the House of Representatives of the United States. The matter about which he writes is one which is presently under review in the United States. In fact, there is now a Bill before Congress with respect to it. What does he say in the letter? He states:
As Members of Congress, we are very concerned that the safety of the air traffic control system is dangerously stressed because of the inexperience of a large percentage of our current controller force.
The problems in our air traffic control system are very real and they are to the point where passenger safety is being directly affected. We have a system stretched beyond its human capacity and an FAA unwilling to even acknowledge that serious problems exist.
That is what he says about the air traffic control situation in the United States. Whay I have just read from is a letter sent to the President of the United States petitioning him to provide immediately an additional 1,000 air traffic controllers in that country. The problem with respect to air traffic controllers was exacerbated by a strike of controllers who were later fired by the President of the United States.

I can tell the Hon. Member what everyone in the United States told us. They told us we cannot begin to contemplate going to a deregulated environment with anyone

speechtext:
We decided as a caucus in December to no longer paticipate in the process of completing that report because Government Members would not allow us the opportunity to record our dissent to a number of the recommendations. We felt in all good conscience as New Democrats that we could not have our names aligned with the White Paper Freedom to Move. Change, Choice, Challenge without having some kind of clear indication as to where we stood on the recommendations made within it. We asked, as did the Liberals in committee, first to have the votes recorded, when that failed we asked for an opportunity to have a dissenting report as part of the majority report by Party and finally, to allow individuals to include dissenting opinions. Those three options were turned down, even though, in terms of the latter two, there were precedents in Parliament of standing committees making those kinds of provisions. I say sincerely that it was with great regret-and we said it at committee-that the Hon. Member for Regina West and I withdrew from the Standing Committee on Transport. Immediately after we made that decision, the Liberal Party decided to follow suit.
The report is a report of Conservative Members. Granted there was a lot of movement, a lot of discussion and a lot of good debate about the principles contained within the report along with the recommendations. I give credit to the Conservative Members of the committee who in many cases were prepared to listen with open ears and open minds and to be
Committee Reports
convinced that something was not appropriate. However, when it came down to the recommendations, we just felt that we could not play any more.
In the time available to me, I want to deal with some of the specific items in the report and to respond accordingly. So far today we have heard many times about the question of safety. The Government was very consistent in saying that safety was not negotiable. As far as the Government of Canada was concerned, safety was not an item on the table. We heard witnesses who suggested otherwise because when it comes to economic reregulation or deregulation there has to be an impact upon safety. I will give two examples. Currently in Canada there is some ongoing testing for an end of train unit to replace the caboose. This device would monitor certain functions of the railway to determine the safety of the train. The railroads argue that that is an economic decision, that they should have the right to make those kinds of changes in their operations because it is cheaper for them to operate. On the other hand the unions and those who provide the human service of monitoring the movement of trains, as well as others in Canada including the New Democratic Party, believe that it is a safety consideration. Under deregulation there would be no mechnanism. If a railroad decided that it would make an economic change, it could do it without having to consult or without having to apply to a regulatory body to ensure that proper hearings were held.
During our hearings in Vancouver we heard that safety was a matter of negotiation between unions and employers. We heard from Ms. Douglas, general chairperson of the Canadian Air Line Flight Attendants Association. She said:
It pains me even to say it, but we have a proposal on the bargaining table; we are trying to negotiate smoke detectors in the washrooms. We have to try to negotiate it, because they cost money.
Also we heard in the testimony that in the negotiations flight attendants were asked by collective agreement to work longer shifts, perhaps to work as long as 18 hours continuously. Ms. Douglas responded as follows:
Contrary to popular belief, flight attendants are not there just to be friendly and serve meals. That is certainly part of our job, but the basic premise for having flight attendants on the aircraft at all is safety ... Other than in-flight problems which might arise, the times when flight attendants should be at their peak-when there are most likely to be problems-are on take-offs and landings.
After a 14-hour duty day, your efficiency certainly drags. Pacific Western also has a proposal on the table to take away or substantially reduce the meals provided for flight attendants on the aircraft, so we work 14 hours and do not have meal breaks and have less in the way of meals and then be called upon at the end of a 14-hour duty day to perhaps have to evacuate an aircraft. That depends-in our training, we have 90 seconds in which to evacuate an aircraft safely before the possibility of smoke and fire makes an accident unsurvivable. So seconds count. Exhaustion at that point in time will cost lives.
Even when we talk about economic deregulation, it will have an impact on safety. All the inspectors and safety regulations which we can provide will not change that aspect. We heard from a number of charter groups which were concerned about the impact of economic deregulation on their operations. Questions were raised about a marginal airline or small feeder line which has not had a real good go at it. I am talking about lines which are close to the wire in terms of bank managers

January 29, 1986
Committee Reports
knocking at their doors and of running marginally for the last month or two. What can the last passenger on the last flight expect? What kind of shape will that aircraft be in? What corners will the company have had to cut in order to continue to operate? The reality is that we will probably not know until the first accident what part was not replaced earlier, what part was kept until the so-called standard date but was really stretched to the limit and failed when it was needed the most. We have to look at those questions.
I should like to turn briefly to the impact of deregulation on the trucking industry. I will particularly focus on northern communities which depend almost totally upon trucking for receipt of their consumer goods or perhaps the movement of products out of there in small volumes. We heard from the trucking industry-the Canadian Trucking Association, the British Columbia association and the Ontario association. One after another they indicated clearly that what would happen under a deregulated environment to smaller, isolated communities would be that service would go down and prices would go up. In British Columbia we were told that some of those communities would not get service because it would be uneconomical for them to continue to provide once or twice a week service to some B.C. communities. Right now it is uneconomical, but because of the regulatory regime there is a trade-off, what we call cross-subsidization where a company obtains a licence to travel from point A or point B, which is the bulk of the market, to larger centres. As a condition of the licence it has to provide a decent level of service to the smaller communities in between. The community of Atikokan in my riding relies totally on trucking for consumer goods. That community is already hard pressed because of the closure of mines and a downturn in their economy. Communities such as that will find themselves paying even more for the goods they need for their daily lives.
Let us take a look at employment. What is the impact on the industry as a result of deregulation? Currently close to three-quarters of a million Canadians are working in this sector. Any change will affect a large portion of the population. Eleven labour organizations appeared before the committee. Each expressed fears that the deregulation proposals would result in substantial job loss and reduced wages for their members. From the Canadian Labour Congress we heard that it was not confident that it would be able to escape being the chief victim of transport deregulation in Canada.
We have, as of yet, very little evidence for the Canadian scene. However, there is a fair bit of knowledge about what happened in the United States. Since 1980, 40,000 Americans in the airline industry lost their jobs. One hundred and fifty thousand jobs disappeared in the railway industry. The best guess for the trucking industry in the United States is that between 250,000 and 300,000 union members were put out of work in this sector and not replaced.
Earlier we had a discussion about confidential contracts and their impact on the transportation industry. One of the realities of American confidential contracts is that potash from the Canadian Prairies can be railed right through to Chicago via the United States lines at a cost cheaper than railing it on CN or CP to Thunder Bay, using Canadian workers, having money stay in Canada, and then shipped by boat to Chicago, again using Canadian workers, returning profits to Canada. If we allow ourselves to move in the direction of confidential contracts we are going to see more and more of that. We are going to see more north-south traffic and less east-west. We are going to see products moving from British Columbia by rail through the United States and back up through Detroit and Windsor, bypassing Canada almost entirely. We do not accept that. We do not think we can allow that kind of change, because we are such a big country. We must have our own environment. We have to ensure that Canadians can work and transport our goods and services across Canada. We should not be setting up a regime that will allow us to bypass most of this country and create the jobs south of the border.
I want to deal more with the air transportation side. I believe ordinary Canadians who feel that deregulation is a great thing are seeing it from the perspective of cheap seats, of the ability to fly from community A to community B at a reasonable price. I cannot blame them for wanting reduced prices. What the Canadian public does not realize is that those cheap seats are only available for consumers in the major transportation corridors. They are not available for those small theatre routes. They are not available across the North. They also are not aware that the bottom has been reached in terms of cheap seats. We heard testimony from officials of Air Canada and Canadian Pacific that prices are as low as they are going to go. There may be some adjustment for some first class or full-fare passengers, but not to any great extent. We want to see those advantages given to all Canadians.
In our Halifax hearings the Harmon Corporation of Ste-phenville, Newfoundland, presented us with some evidence from the United States. I just want to very quickly quote from it. This was a statement by a Richard B. Keinz, Assistant Commissioner, Minnesota Department of Transportation, Aeronautics Division before the Subcommittee on Aviation, Committee on Public Works and Transportation, House of Representatives, on June 9, 1983. They spoke about the experience in the State of Minnesota of deregulation. With regard to air fares he stated:
Deregulation has introduced an opportunity for airlines to offer a variety of air fares. In the monopoly or single carrier markets, the variety appears to be mostly of the high variety.
In other words, after you clean out the competition and you get it down so that you are the only carrier, you decide what the market will bear and you boost the costs. We recognize that economics is a factor in setting fares. However, we have a difficult time rationalizing why it costs 4 cents to 20 cents per mile to transport a passenger from New York to Los Angeles as compared to 14 cents to 20 cents per mile to carry a passenger between Boston and Los Angeles, or 17 cents to 21 cents per mile to carry a passenger between Minneapolis and St. Paul and Los Angeles. In some cases it goes up as much as
January 29, 1986

$1 a mile. Clearly, there is a lot to learn from the United States experience. History has always pointed out that we should learn from our mistakes. We should also learn from other's mistakes. When, at the end of my comments, I move a motion, I will do so because 1 think the Standing Committee on Transport needs more time. We need time to travel to northern Canada. We need time to travel to those other provinces we did not have an opportunity to visit. We need time to visit the United States to speak to people who are key players in the aviation industry, the trucking industry and, the rail industry to learn from them how we can do better in a deregulated environment.
In conclusion, I would like to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That the sixth report be not now concurred in but that it be recommitted to the Standing Committee of Transport for further consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to say how pleased I am to enter this debate, notwithstanding the fact that the issue has been brought to the floor of the House in a rather convoluted and unorthodox fashion. First members of the NDP moved to concur and then moved not to concur. Notwithstanding that, 1 think it is a timely debate and a good one and I will try to stick to the thrust of the motion and cover some of the elements of the sixth report, the subject before us.
I have heard from various speakers that we have not had enough time to deal with this important issue and that it is such an important issue that it should be considered in detail. I would have thought that the House would have been packed today but most of the time there have been three or four Liberal Members and three or four NDP Members present. One wonders sometimes and has to question the sincerity of their bringing this motion forward when it seems to be filled with more rhetoric than genuine concern.
Notwithstanding that, I wish to begin by paying tribute to all Hon. Members who served on the standing committee. I know that this report does not necessarily reflect only the opinions of Progressive Conservative Members. I know other Members had a part to play in drafting the recommendations and I know they worked very hard under a very tight time frame. The report that has been brought forth is realistic and thoughtful and I must say that it is very valuable to those of us who are charged with the next phase of this process, the drafting of the legislation. I believe this is another clear step in the evolution of a new transportation framework. By all accounts, we recognize that the transportation framework needs to be overhauled.
I would like to compliment the chairman of the standing committee on the very eloquent and well reasoned speech he made today putting into context the proceedings at the standing committee and describing the events that took place. I also want to compliment him on the fact that never before have there been such a number of witnesses heard in such a short period of time and their evidence digested in such a comprehensive fashion. Something in the order of 95 witnesses were heard and 172 briefs were submitted. As the Hon. Member pointed out, after looking at that many briefs and hearing that many submissions, things become somewhat repetitious. I believe the views that were presented were presented quite clearly right across the country.
As has been pointed out in the committee report, the committee's deliberation was only one phase of this process. I find this debate to be rather strange, particularly since Liberal Members are criticizing this process. I have been around here for a long time and this is the first time I have seen a policy document come before a standing committee of the House for a full-fleged debate and a comprehensive analysis before the drafting process began.

January 29, 1986
Committee Reports
This process started last February when I invited everyone in Canada who is interested in transportation to engage in the debate and the process of regulatory reform. I invited them to engage in the process of rewriting the National Transportation Act and putting in place a new legislative and regulatory framework. I said: "Let us have your views and thoughts. Either see us personally, send in a formalized brief, give us a telephone call or write it on the back of an envelope, but we want to hear from you". We heard from people from coast to coast. We sent people across the country to listen to special interest groups, to provinces and to labour groups. When we put the Freedom to Move paper together and released it in July for further public debate. We released it to the Standing Committee on Transport and now we are engaged in the process of writing the legislation.
This is a new process and I think it is working. 1 find it rather strange that Hon. Members would be complaining about time. They will still have all kinds of time when it comes to dealing with the actual legislation. However, surely there comes a time when we have to stop consulting and start drafting the legislation. We will certainly be entertaining the thoughts, suggestions and proposed amendments of Hon. Members when we deal with the legislation.
Surely now is the time to act. If Hon. Members want another mandate to study the legislation, I am sure that can be arranged. I believe that we all want to have the best piece of legislation that can possibly be delivered, legislation that is in the best interests of the Parliament of Canada and Canadians as a whole and indeed in the best interests of transportation.
A great many recommendations were made and I will not be able to touch on all of them. Some of the more important issues such as service to northern and remote areas are matters we are considering very seriously. A modified non-compensatory rail rate scheme, the role of transportation as a tool for economic development and the issue of foreign ownership in the transportation system are all items that are under active consideration.
On balance, I can say that the recommendations that are contained in the sixth report of the standing committee can be accommodated in a general way. There may be some details on which we may not agree but generally speaking we agree with the thrust of the recommendations and I think that Hon. Members will find many of the recommendations woven into the legislation when it is introduced to the House.
Hon. Members want more time. Perhaps we need more time to deal with some aspects of the issue but the fact is that it is time now to bring on the legislation. Canada's transportation network has reached a critical junction. We believe very firmly that we must overhaul our legislative and regulatory framework in order to achieve the kind of economic development we need. At the present time, we sense that the regulatory transportation regime that is in place represents an obstacle and indeed it is a burden on the economy. Quite frankly, we believe that it stifles growth and innovation and has prevented the system from providing the best service to the Canadian people. In fact, the other day I heard an airline executive say that
under the current regulatory system, they have been more preoccupied with satisfying the regulator rather than the customer. Surely that must change and that is what we are trying to do. This will not be a revolution. Much of this has already taken place and what we are doing now is putting in place the regulatory and legislative mechanisms to authorize what has already been taken place for wuite some time.
In a recent report entitled The Canadian Common Market, the Canada West Foundation stated this regarding trucking:
-"the chaotic welter of provincial trucking regulations make it an administrative nightmare to move goods by truck across provincial boundaries and therefore impede the movement of goods".
That is not a political statement. It did not come from us. It came from a study team from western Canada. There are a myriad of regulations regarding trucking. There are 10 different regulations in each province and then there is another set of regulations thrust upon the trucking industry by the federal Government. There must be a move toward greater uniformity in the regulatory mechanisms covering the moving of goods from province to province.
I am sorry that the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has just left the Chamber. He knows the effectiveness of the current appeal mechanisms under the National Transportation Act and, in particular, the captive shipper clause. For example, one appeal under Section 23 of the NTA took seven years to hear. Another case launched under Section 278 of the Railway Act took nearly eight years to be acted upon. I would like to say that there was only one such case in 20 years. That is clearly not satisfactory. Clearly, the desire and demand for reform is there and we are acting upon it.
I would like to point out other regulations to Hon. Members. Section 230 allows the Governor in Council to make by-laws governing spitting on trains. Nothing is wrong with spitting; but if one misses the spittoon one could be fined $40.

Sure, we will learn from the experience of others. There is no question about that. We are not talking about massive deregulation; we are talking about regulatory reform. We are talking about changing the legislative framework and the regulatory framework in such a way that it will take into consideration the uniqueness of Canada, our economy, our social infrastructure and our demography. These are factors which we will try to harmonize with the real facts of Canadian life. We are not copying the United States holus-bolus. We will learn from the American experience, and from the experience of others. We have heard from a great many people and we have talked with a great many others. Personally, I have gone out across the country. I must say that I have not found any antagonism toward the basic thrust of Freedom to Move. I have spoken to the Calgary Chamber of Commerce, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Summit Conference and the Traffic Club of Montreal Inc. I spoke about this topic during National Transportation Week in Toronto. I have spoken on the topic to the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Roads and Transportation Association of Canada, the Alberta Aviation Council, the Toronto Board of Trade, the Ontario Trucking Association and the Air Transport Association of Canada. I participated in a seminar at Concordia University on the subject. Monday last I spoke to the Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities Association. I have engaged in many panel discussions and many federal-provincial meetings on the topic. Our officials have also engaged in many federal-provincial meetings in which the basic points of contention were dealt with. We have tried to find a way to resolve them together in a consultative fashion.
The Hon. Member for Regina West talked about this being an ideological knee-jerk reaction. I must say that I find nothing more knee-jerk, in terms of an ideological reaction, than the comment which I suspect he is the author of found at page 26 which states: "We are philosophically opposed to confidential contracts". And he talks about us being philosophically hooked and reacting in a knee-jerk fashion! How can he say this when the CTC has gone out across the land in a very comprehensive fashion and has examined the issue of confidential contracting? As a matter of fact, the Commission examined the issue of confidential contracting, both on transborder traffic and, indeed, on domestic traffic. The Canadian Transport Commission's extensive deliberations and reports into these matters took some 18 days of public hearings. A second hearing held on the same subject yielded 77 submissions and
3,000	pages of transcript. It turned out to be a 19-day hearing.
I failed to mention that in addition to the debate which has been taking place here, and in other places in the country, not to mention within the industry, there has been a rather interesting debate ongoing with the CTC. It was the instigator of this process. The CTC has engaged in a number of hearings at
Committee Reports
which this matter was studied. Many of the recommendations of the CTC have been incorporated into this document.
We have all heard about the near unanimous support for the main thurst of economic reform. Even the Hon. Member for Regina West in a radio interview had to admit, and I quote: "I'd say a majority of the briefs so far have been in favour." Right on. There is no question about that.
Members of the Liberal Party brought down their own report. I had a chance to reread it last night. I have never seen anything so hollow, so inconsistent and so blended with contradictions. It is really quite consistent with what we are hearing from Members opposite. I would just like to touch briefly upon a couple of items because they make one chuckle. First, at page 9, they state that the Liberal Party does not support deregulation of the trucking industry at this time. That is strange since I have in front of me a number of quotations from the former Minister of Transport. One of them states:
The next deregulatory salvos will be fired at the end of the month when Axworthy meets with the provinces to look at trucking. These talks follow meetings in January when Axworthy and provincial officials discussed ways to establish uniformity in trucking regulations-
That is a quote from The Financial Time of May 21, 1984.
In front of me I have another article entitled "One trump" which states:

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate which has been waging for the last several hours on the deregulation of our transportation industry. Toward that end I would like to focus the bulk of my remarks on the airline industry. We all know that the policy of deregulation is based on the report produced by the Government entitled Freedom to Move. I think it is very crucial, significant, and relevant to point out that this document took 15 months to prepare. It took 15 months to put the themes, proposals, and philosophies guiding this document on to paper. By comparison, this document has only been in the hands of the Transport Committee, which was asked to examine it and call public hearings on it, for two months.
I suggest that from a logical point of view, and from the point of view of Canadian tradition, that that somehow does not wash. I admit, as does my Party, that the airline industry and the transportation industry in general is in need of reform. It needs reform to cope with the new and evolving aspirations that we see around us. However, I suggest with all due respect that one cannot embark on a new and bold initiative which took some 15 months to put together, and then have only two months to examine it from a public opinion point of view. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) alluded to that when he said that the committee had a very short time to deal with this issue. There were some 92 interventions and 150 submissions to the committee and if there is that much interest, and there is, then two months is not sufficient to deal with it.
Another point I want to make concerns the statement that deregulation is going to benefit the consumer. The consumer will be paying less to move from point A to point B. That is an attractive feature. Obviously all Members have to be concerned over what it means for the consumer. If it means reduced airline fares, then we have to be very cognizant of that fact. However, we also have to be fair, honest and truthful and really look into this report. The Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) indicated the problems consumers have been having in the U.S. under deregulation. That country moved in 1978 to deregulation and up until 1984 U.S. airlines lost some $4 billion. Service in some remote areas has become irregular or non-existent. As well, the cost of air fares in those more remote parts of the country have increased.
We have seen companies in the U.S. go belly-up because they tried to expand too quickly or because they misread their own capabilities. Other companies, with an eye on their bottom lines, stopped serving a given community with only 60 days notice. How does that help the consumer? Those factors have to be taken into account before we can honestly say that the consumer will win or lose under deregulation. As well, a lot of the larger airlines in the U.S. have bought up smaller airlines which got into trouble under deregulation. How has that profited the consumer?
Deregulation was supposed to mean a greater opportunity for more airlines to create more competition. What is happening? In some markets these airlines are creating monopolies. We have seen that in our country even without deregulation. Canadian Pacific has purchased Nordair and Eastern Provincial. Air Canada owns a portion of Air Ontario. Under deregulation we can expect more such takeovers. What started as an attempt to loosen up the system, to provide more flexibility, more opportunity and lessen the monopoly some carriers have, has evolved into something worse, and it can happen here.
As well, Mr. Speaker, when we talk about the problems of service to remote areas in the U.S., we can expect even more of a problem in Canada. Canada is a very large country with its population centres spotted irregularly across the land. We have to look beyond the sixtieth parallel at the people in Yellow-
January 29, 1986

knife, Cambridge Bay and Coppermine. Those people do not look to air carriers only for transportation, they look to them to bring in their food and carry out the goods they produce.
If we look at the Toronto-Ottawa or Toronto-Montreal routes, that is one question. But if we look at Toronto-Yellowknife, then it is a totally different matter. We are talking about what this country is about. We are talking about the contact that each and every Canadian has with his country. Our carriers have a responsibility to serve the smaller communities and sparsely-populated areas of our country. However, if we go head first into deregulation what is going to happen to those communities? Is it the bottom line that will dictate whether an airline serves a particular community? If so, we will not have the same kind of country we have now and let's make no bones about that.
We have to learn from the U.S. experience, which brings us to another issue, that of safety. How often do we get up in this House to mourn a tragic accident after it happens? How many times do we say we should take precautions and try to avoid the accident in the first place? Well, here we have a golden opportunity to avoid asking ourselves that question repeatedly. The Hon.
